claim: Adult neurogenesis continues in the mammalian hippocampus, including that of humans throughout life.
source: Accumulating evidence has revealed that neurogenesis continues in the mammalian hippocampus, including that of humans throughout life (Déry et al., 2013; Spalding et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Déry et al., 2013 and Spalding et al., 2013.

claim: Neurons generated in the dentate gyrus (DG) area of the hippocampus during adulthood mature into dentate granule cells (DGCs).
source: Neurons generated in the dentate gyrus (DG) area of the hippocampus during adulthood mature into dentate granule cells (DGCs), which can integrate into existing hippocampal neural circuits (Toni et al., 2008; Gu et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Toni et al., 2008 and Gu et al., 2012.

claim: Adult-born dentate granule cells can integrate into existing hippocampal neural circuits.
source: Neurons generated in the dentate gyrus (DG) area of the hippocampus during adulthood mature into dentate granule cells (DGCs), which can integrate into existing hippocampal neural circuits (Toni et al., 2008; Gu et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Toni et al., 2008 and Gu et al., 2012.

claim: Adult-born dentate granule cells influence affective states or cognitive processes.
source: Neurons generated in the dentate gyrus (DG) area of the hippocampus during adulthood mature into dentate granule cells (DGCs), which can integrate into existing hippocampal neural circuits (Toni et al., 2008; Gu et al., 2012) and influence affective states or cognitive processes (Santarelli et al., 2003; Snyder et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Santarelli et al., 2003 and Snyder et al., 2011.

claim: Inhibition of adult neurogenesis profoundly influences performance in certain hippocampal dependent tasks, such as those that assess spatial pattern separation and cognitive flexibility.
source: In particular, recent studies applying pharmacogenetic and optogenetic tools to inhibit adult neurogenesis have demonstrated how this population of new cells can profoundly influence performance in certain hippocampal dependent tasks, such as those that assess spatial pattern separation and cognitive flexibility (Clelland et al., 2009; Gu et al., 2012; Swan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clelland et al., 2009, Gu et al., 2012, and Swan et al., 2014.

claim: Adult born dentate granule cells continue their morphological development for an extended period of time, often over months in rodents and years in primates.
source: While adult born dentate granule cells (abDGCs) continue their morphological development for an extended period of time, often over months in rodents and years in primates (Ge et al., 2007; Kohler et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ge et al., 2007 and Kohler et al., 2011.

claim: There is a transient maturation period corresponding to the first several weeks of integration when adult-born dentate granule cells exhibit heightened membrane excitability and elevated potential for synaptic plasticity.
source: there is a transient maturation period corresponding to the first several weeks of integration when they exhibit heightened membrane excitability and elevated potential for synaptic plasticity (Ge et al., 2007; Marín-Burgin et al., 2012; Dieni et al., 2013; Kropff et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ge et al., 2007, Marín-Burgin et al., 2012, Dieni et al., 2013, and Kropff et al., 2015.

claim: The biophysical properties of young abDGCs during their highly excitable critical developmental window may be uniquely suited to facilitate the computational aspects that underlie pattern separation by influencing larger networks.
source: The biophysical properties of young abDGCs, during their highly excitable critical developmental window may be uniquely suited to facilitate the computational aspects that underlie pattern separation by influencing larger networks (Sahay et al., 2011a, 2011b; Yassa and Stark, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sahay et al., 2011a, 2011b, and Yassa and Stark, 2011.

claim: Young abDGCs may be easily excited by entorhinal inputs that recruit distinct neuronal ensembles, and thus constitute a unique pattern of activity required for pattern separation.
source: It is plausible, for example, that young abDGCs may be easily excited by entorhinal inputs that recruit distinct neuronal ensembles, and thus constitute a unique pattern of activity required for pattern separation (Ge et al., 2007; Sahay et al., 2011b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ge et al., 2007 and Sahay et al., 2011b.

claim: abDGCs with presumed higher baseline firing rates may contribute to pattern separation by non-selectively driving global feedback inhibition via hilar interneurons, thereby creating a sparse firing state within the DG.
source: Alternatively, abDGCs with presumed higher baseline firing rates may contribute to pattern separation by non-selectively driving global feedback inhibition via hilar interneurons, thereby creating a sparse firing state within the DG, in which only the strongest or most highly trained inputs can overcome local inhibition (Jung and McNaughton, 1993; Alme et al., 2010; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2012; Ikrar et al., 2013; Piatti et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jung and McNaughton, 1993, Alme et al., 2010, Neunuebel and Knierim, 2012, Ikrar et al., 2013, and Piatti et al., 2013.

claim: Pattern separation refers to a computational process of forming distinct representations of similar inputs via unique ensembles of neurons, which could facilitate memory encoding by minimizing interference.
source: Pattern separation refers to a computational process of forming distinct representations of similar inputs via unique ensembles of neurons, which could facilitate memory encoding by minimizing interference (Sahay et al., 2011b; Yassa and Stark, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sahay et al., 2011b and Yassa and Stark, 2011.

claim: The DG can perform pattern separation as a consequence of the sparse firing properties of its cells and the large number of dentate cells compared to both its upstream and downstream regions.
source: It has been hypothesized that the DG can perform this function as a consequence of the sparse firing properties of its cells and the large number of dentate cells compared to both its upstream and downstream regions (Treves and Rolls, 1994; Leutgeb et al., 2007; Yassa and Stark, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Treves and Rolls, 1994, Leutgeb et al., 2007, and Yassa and Stark, 2011.

claim: Selective lesions of the DG but not CA1 or CA3 impaired rats' ability to discriminate between locations in spatial discrimination tasks.
source: For example, selective lesions of the DG but not CA1 or CA3 impaired rats' ability to discriminate between locations in spatial discrimination tasks (Treves and Rolls, 1994; Leutgeb et al., 2007; Yassa and Stark, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Treves and Rolls, 1994, Leutgeb et al., 2007, and Yassa and Stark, 2011.

claim: Increases in blood-oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) signal in the DG is highly correlated with the pattern separation process in humans.
source: Studies in humans have also shown that increases in blood-oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) signal in the DG is highly correlated with the pattern separation process (Bakker et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bakker et al., 2008.

claim: Chronic increases or decreases of adult neurogenesis have provided consistent results in behavioral tasks designed to test abilities that are thought to depend on pattern separation.
source: Interestingly, even though the impact of adult neurogenesis on other hippocampal-dependent behaviors remains controversial (Clelland et al., 2009; Deng et al., 2010; Sahay et al., 2011a; Kesner, 2013), chronic increases or decreases of adult neurogenesis have provided consistent results in behavioral tasks designed to test abilities that are thought to depend on pattern separation (Clelland et al., 2009; Sahay et al., 2011a; Kesner et al., 2014; Rangel et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clelland et al., 2009, Sahay et al., 2011a, Kesner et al., 2014, and Rangel et al., 2014.

claim: Retroviruses specifically integrate into newly divided cells making them an optimal technique for targeting neurogenesis.
source: Retroviruses are known to specifically integrate into newly divided cells making them an optimal technique for targeting neurogenesis.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about retroviral properties.

claim: The vast majority of newly divided cells in the subgranular zone will go on to become granule cells.
source: In the central nervous system, the vast majority of newly divided cells in the subgranular zone will go on to become granule cells (Kuhn et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kuhn et al., 1996.

claim: 2.5 ± 1.5% of all EDU-labeled cells co-localized with the GFP transgene delivered via MSCV in animals given EdU injections three days post-viral injection.
source: We found that 2.5 ± 1.5% of all EDU-labeled cells co-localized with the GFP transgene delivered via MSCV in animals given EdU injections three days post-viral injection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from EdU co-localization studies.

claim: 0.5 ± 0.3% of all EdU-labeled cells co-localized with GFP for animals given EdU injections on day seven post-virus.
source: This number fell to 0.5 ± 0.3% of all EdU-labeled cells for animals given EdU injections on day seven post-virus (n = 3 mice for each group).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from EdU co-localization studies.

claim: The MSCV retrovirus construct drove expression of ArchT-GFP uniquely in cells that were undergoing division during the short period following viral delivery.
source: This finding also validates that our MSCV retrovirus construct drove expression of ArchT-GFP uniquely in cells that were undergoing division during the short period following viral delivery, consistent with other retroviral studies (Faulkner et al., 2008; Toni et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Faulkner et al., 2008 and Toni et al., 2008.

claim: Among GFP-expressing cells examined two weeks after viral injections, almost all exhibited clear neuronal morphology.
source: Among GFP-expressing cells examined two weeks after viral injections, almost all exhibited clear neuronal morphology, consistent with the preferred neuronal targeting properties of the synapsin promoter (Nathanson et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and citation to Nathanson et al., 2009.

claim: Labeled abDGCs imaged 30–60 days post injection showed typical dentate cell morphology.
source: Labeled abDGCs imaged 30–60 days post injection showed typical dentate cell morphology (Figure 1B, C) (Zhao et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B, C and citation to Zhao et al., 2006.

claim: ArchT-GFP expression was well targeted to the plasma membrane and remained strong in animals tested as far out as eight months post-viral injection.
source: ArchT-GFP expression was well targeted to the plasma membrane and remained strong in animals tested as far out as eight months post-viral injection (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The location discrimination task has been shown to be sensitive to hippocampal lesions.
source: This task was designed to quantitatively measure the animal's ability to discriminate between two objects separated spatially from one another across various distances (Figure 2A), and has been shown to be sensitive to hippocampal lesions (McTighe et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McTighe et al., 2009.

claim: The location discrimination task has been shown to be sensitive to chronic ablation of adult neurogenesis using x-ray irradiation.
source: This task was designed to quantitatively measure the animal's ability to discriminate between two objects separated spatially from one another across various distances (Figure 2A), and has been shown to be sensitive to hippocampal lesions (McTighe et al., 2009) or chronic ablation of adult neurogenesis using x-ray irradiation (Clelland et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Clelland et al., 2009.

claim: Mice needed fewer trials to complete the block in the easy separation condition relative to the difficult separation condition.
source: In addition, consistent with previous studies (Clelland et al., 2009; Oomen et al., 2013), mice needed fewer trials to complete the block in the easy separation condition relative to the difficult separation condition (trials needed in easy separation: 16.0 ± 0.4; in difficult separation: 20.7 ± 1.0, p<0.01, n = 10 mice, paired t-test comparing the baseline blocks in easy versus difficult separation conditions).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Clelland et al., 2009 and Oomen et al., 2013.

claim: The ArchT-GFP group showed selective impairment in performing the difficult separation when light was delivered to young abDGCs (5–10 weeks of maturation), requiring more trials to complete the illumination blocks.
source: On trials where we delivered light to young abDGCs (5–10 weeks of maturation), the ArchT-GFP group showed selective impairment in performing the difficult separation, requiring more trials to complete the illumination blocks, but performed equally well as control mice under the easy separation condition (Figure 2Ci).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2Ci.

claim: The ArchT-GFP group performed equally well as control mice under the easy separation condition when light was delivered to young abDGCs.
source: On trials where we delivered light to young abDGCs (5–10 weeks of maturation), the ArchT-GFP group showed selective impairment in performing the difficult separation, requiring more trials to complete the illumination blocks, but performed equally well as control mice under the easy separation condition (Figure 2Ci).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2Ci.

claim: No differences in reaction time were found across the two groups, suggesting that optogenetic silencing of abDGCs is important for modulating the cognitive aspects of the task directly as opposed to influencing locomotion.
source: We found no differences in reaction time, defined as time from trial initiation to window selection, across the two groups suggesting that optogenetic silencing of abDGCs is important for modulating the cognitive aspects of the task directly as opposed to influencing locomotion for example.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on reaction time measurements.

claim: Young abDGCs play an essential role in discriminating narrowly separated spatial locations.
source: These results also provide strong evidence that young abDGCs play an essential role in discriminating narrowly separated spatial locations, consistent with the theory of the DG's described role as a pattern separator.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing impairment in difficult separation tasks.

claim: Transient silencing of young abDGCs during the last 5 s of the ITI had no effect on behavioral performance.
source: To examine whether young abDGCs are selectively involved during the performing phase of the task, or have a more general role in task engagement, we transiently silenced the same abDGCs during the last 5 s of the ITI, and found no effect on behavioral performance in those blocks (Figure 2Ciii).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2Ciii.

claim: Young abDGCs are specifically required during the choice phase of the task.
source: This result demonstrates that young abDGCs are specifically required during the choice phase of the task.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing no effect during ITI silencing.

claim: Transient silencing of young abDGCs produced a significant reduction in single trial performance.
source: To further evaluate the impact of abDGCs on task performance during a given trial, we examined the success rate in trials when light was delivered. We found that transient silencing of young abDGCs also produced a significant reduction in single trial performance (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Adult neurogenesis is critical for online information processing during spatial discrimination.
source: Together, these results suggest that adult neurogenesis is critical for online information processing during spatial discrimination.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing immediate effects of silencing on performance.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of older abDGCs (14–18 weeks of maturation) had no impact on behavioral performance in any of the separation conditions.
source: Optogenetic silencing of older abDGCs (14–18 weeks of maturation) had no impact on behavioral performance in any of the separation conditions (Figure 2Civ).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2Civ.

claim: No significant loss of neurons was found in the retest group relative to performing animals that underwent quantification at 10 weeks post-infusion.
source: To determine if the inability of older cells to influence behavioral performance could be a result of neuronal loss, we quantified the number of labeled abDGCs at these early and late phases following virus injection. We found no significant loss of neurons in this group of animals relative to performing animals that underwent quantification at 10 weeks post-infusion (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Although a significant number of abDGCs degenerate within the first couple weeks of birth, little degeneration occurs beyond 4 weeks of age.
source: This finding is consistent with the observation that although a significant number of abDGCs degenerate within the first couple weeks of birth, little degeneration occurs beyond 4 weeks of age (Dayer et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Dayer et al., 2003.

claim: A set of age-defined abDGCs that are highly effective in modulating LD performance when young have comparatively weaker effects on performance at later developmental stages.
source: Whether the observed loss of behavioral impact during retest could be due to a slight reduction in cell number, or changes in the intrinsic excitability or synaptic targeting properties of the same number of cells; our results provide direct longitudinal evidence that a set of age-defined abDGCs that are highly effective in modulating LD performance when young, have comparatively weaker effects on performance at later developmental stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from longitudinal testing.

claim: abDGCs exhibit differing levels of influence on behavior across maturation.
source: This is consistent with the general observation that abDGCs exhibit differing levels of influence on behavior across maturation (Gu et al., 2012; Nakashiba et al., 2012; Swan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gu et al., 2012, Nakashiba et al., 2012, and Swan et al., 2014.

claim: POMC-Arch mice express the optogenetic silencer Arch in all dentate granule cells, including both developmentally-born and adult-born cells.
source: POMC-Arch mice express the optogenetic silencer Arch in all dentate granule cells, including both developmentally-born and adult-born cells, and the expression of ArchT in each cell persists permanently throughout the animal's life. (McHugh et al., 2007; Madisen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McHugh et al., 2007 and Madisen et al., 2012.

claim: Optogenetic silencing in POMC-Arch mice did not produce a behavioral deficit during the easy separation condition.
source: In addition, optogenetic silencing in POMC-Arch mice did not produce a behavioral deficit during the easy separation condition (Figure 3B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The DG is required only for separating spatial locations that are finely delineated, but not for locations that are broadly dissociated.
source: In addition, optogenetic silencing in POMC-Arch mice did not produce a behavioral deficit during the easy separation condition (Figure 3B), confirming that the DG is required only for separating spatial locations that are finely delineated, but not for locations that are broadly dissociated, consistent with the general observation of the importance of the DG in behavioral tasks testing pattern separation (Kesner, 2013) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and citation to Kesner, 2013.

claim: The DG has a critical and ongoing role in spatial discrimination during both the initial test and retest.
source: As silencing in POMC-Arch mice represents complete inhibition of all DGCs simultaneously (including both young and mature neurons), our findings suggest that the DG has a critical and ongoing role in spatial discrimination during both the initial test and retest
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results in POMC-Arch mice.

claim: New young cells continue to support performance throughout the animal's lifetime.
source: As silencing in POMC-Arch mice represents complete inhibition of all DGCs simultaneously (including both young and mature neurons), our findings suggest that the DG has a critical and ongoing role in spatial discrimination during both the initial test and retest, and suggest that new young cells continue to support performance throughout the animal's lifetime.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results in POMC-Arch mice.

claim: The reduced behavioral influence of older abDGCs during retest is unlikely attributed to processes of memory consolation.
source: Further, our findings are supportive of the theory that the reduced behavioral influence of older abDGCs during retest is unlikely attributed to processes of memory consolation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing continued DG involvement during retest.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of young abDGCs (at seven week maturation) led to significant BOLD signal changes within the local DG/CA3 regions, as well as in the contralateral hippocampus.
source: Optogenetic silencing of young abDGCs (at seven week maturation) led to significant BOLD signal changes within the local DG/CA3 regions, as well as in the contralateral hippocampus (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: No BOLD signal changes were detected in the GFP-control group examined with the same opto-fMRI protocols.
source: No BOLD signal changes were detected in the GFP-control group examined with the same opto-fMRI protocols (Figure 4B), confirming that the observed BOLD signals are not due to any potential heat or light artifact (Christie et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 4B and citation to Christie et al., 2013.

claim: The time-course extracted from significantly changed voxels revealed a decrease in BOLD signals in bilateral hippocampal regions.
source: The time-course extracted from significantly changed voxels revealed a decrease in BOLD signals in bilateral hippocampal regions (Figure 4Fi, ii).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 4Fi, ii.

claim: When the same mice were retested at 16 weeks, optogenetic silencing failed to produce any detectable BOLD signal changes.
source: When the same mice were retested at 16 weeks, optogenetic silencing failed to produce any detectable BOLD signal changes (Figure 4D) (Alme et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 4D and citation to Alme et al., 2010.

claim: Opto-fMRI testing in the POMC-Arch transgenic mice showed much stronger reduction in BOLD signals in the local ipsilateral hippocampus compared to that observed upon optogenetic silencing of only young abDGCs.
source: The same opto-fMRI testing in the POMC-Arch transgenic mice showed much stronger reduction in BOLD signals in the local ipsilateral hippocampus compared to that observed upon optogenetic silencing of only young abDGCs (Figure 4E, 4Fiii)
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data shown in Figure 4E and 4Fiii.

claim: No BOLD signals were observed in the contralateral hippocampus in the POMC-Arch mice.
source: Interestingly and surprisingly, we did not observe any BOLD signals in the contralateral hippocampus in the POMC-Arch mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI data.

claim: abDGCs can engage the bilateral hippocampus during early development.
source: Together, these results suggest that abDGCs can engage the bilateral hippocampus during early development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the fMRI results showing bilateral BOLD signal changes.

claim: abDGCs may function through the contralaterally projecting hippocampal neurons that are downstream of the optogenetically silenced abDGCs, such as the hilar mossy cells, CA3 pyramidal cells, or CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: While fMRI cannot directly measure the neural circuits recruited by young abDGCs, anatomical evidence supports the idea that abDGCs may function through the contralaterally projecting hippocampal neurons that are downstream of the optogenetically silenced abDGCs, such as the hilar mossy cells, CA3 pyramidal cells, or CA1 pyramidal cells (Amaral et al., 2007; Toni et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical evidence and citations to Amaral et al., 2007 and Toni et al., 2008.

claim: During optogenetic silencing of young abDGCs, LFPs recorded in the contralateral CA1 region showed robust increases in power at multiple frequency ranges.
source: During optogenetic silencing of young abDGCs, LFPs recorded in the contralateral CA1 region showed robust increases in power at multiple frequency ranges, suggesting significant neural network influences (Figure 5D, middle).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No change in LFPs was observed in the somatosensory cortex or in the CA3 region during optogenetic silencing of young abDGCs.
source: In contrast, no change in LFPs was observed in the somatosensory cortex (400 µm above the identified CA1 region), or in the CA3 region (400 µm below the identified CA1 region, Figure 5D, left and right).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No change in LFP power was observed upon identical analysis in control mice where young abDGCs were labeled with GFP.
source: In addition, no change in LFP power was observed upon identical analysis in control mice where young abDGCs were labeled with GFP, confirming that light illumination alone did not produce any detectable LFP change (Figure 5Ci and 5Cii ).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5Ci and 5Cii.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of young abDGCs selectively increased higher frequency oscillations, such as beta (15–25 Hz), low gamma (30–50 Hz), and high gamma (70–100 Hz) and high frequency oscillations, but not theta frequencies (4–10 Hz).
source: Upon further examination, we discovered that optogenetic silencing of young abDGCs selectively increased higher frequency oscillations, such as beta (15–25 Hz), low gamma (30–50 Hz), and high gamma (70–100 Hz) and high frequency oscillations, but not theta frequencies (4–10 Hz) (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claim: Adult neurogenesis is capable of selectively recruiting the contralateral hippocampal CA1 neural network without increasing LFP synchrony in CA3.
source: These results demonstrate that adult neurogenesis is capable of selectively recruiting the contralateral hippocampal CA1 neural network and this occurs without increasing LFP synchrony in CA3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the electrophysiology results showing CA1 changes without CA3 changes.

claim: Increased activation seen during spatial navigation can promote 30–120 Hz rhythms in CA1 fields without requiring CA3 synchrony at gamma frequencies.
source: It is important to note that increased activation seen during spatial navigation can promote 30–120 Hz rhythms in CA1 fields without requiring CA3 synchrony at gamma frequencies (Middleton and McHugh, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Middleton and McHugh, 2016.

claim: The increase in power builds through the silencing period in ArchT-GFP animals.
source: To further understand this phenomenon, we looked at the relative LFP power temporally across the optogenetic silencing window. We found that the increase in power builds through the silencing period in ArchT-GFP animals [repeated measures ANOVA main effect of time for high frequency: F3,21 = 4.367, p=0.015; high gamma: F3,21 = 4.426, p=0.015; low gamma: F3,21 = 7.230, p=0.002; and beta ranges: F3,21 = 5.255, p=0.007]
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data and statistical analysis.

claim: The increase in strength was significantly higher during the last 2.5 s of silencing relative to the baseline for all frequencies ranges analyzed.
source: Further analysis of the time window revealed that the increase in strength was significantly higher during the last 2.5 s of silencing relative to the baseline for all frequencies ranges analyzed.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data and statistical analysis.

claim: This gradual increase in power was broadly represented across multiple frequency bands and is suggestive of an increase in generalized excitability possibly via reduced inhibition.
source: This gradual increase in power was broadly represented across multiple frequency bands and is suggestive of an increase in generalized excitability possibly via reduced inhibition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the electrophysiology data showing broad frequency increases.

claim: Lacefield et al. reported that a broad overall increase in gamma power (25–80 Hz) in the hippocampus in urethane anesthetized mice that had been x-ray irradiated 6–10 weeks earlier.
source: In support of this theory, Lacefield et al. also reported that a broad overall increase in gamma power (25–80 Hz) in the hippocampus in urethane anesthetized mice that had been x-ray irradiated 6–10 weeks earlier.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lacefield et al., 2012.

claim: The increase in gamma power in irradiated mice was dependent on perforant pathway inputs.
source: Further, they determined this increase was dependent on perforant pathway inputs (2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lacefield et al., 2012.

claim: Chronic ablation of adult neurogenesis altered hippocampal oscillatory patterns.
source: Our findings with optogenetic silencing are also consistent with other studies of chronic ablation of adult neurogenesis in that newborn cell silencing altered hippocampal oscillatory patterns (Lacefield et al., 2012; Rangel et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lacefield et al., 2012 and Rangel et al., 2013.

claim: The effect of abDGC silencing on hippocampal oscillations occurs immediately and is not a compensatory effect.
source: Our findings add to this discussion by revealing that this effect occurs immediately and is not a compensatory effect
evidence: The claim is inferred from the immediate effects observed during optogenetic silencing.

claim: The DG contributes only to a subset of the oscillators within the hippocampus.
source: Our findings add to this discussion by revealing that this effect occurs immediately and is not a compensatory effect and are supportive of the conclusion that the DG contributes only to a subset of the oscillators within the hippocampus (Kocsis et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kocsis et al., 1999.

claim: Oscillations represent coordinated interactions of excitation and inhibition in a circuit that may create optimal windows for communication.
source: As oscillations represent coordinated interactions of excitation and inhibition in a circuit that may create optimal windows for communication, the ability for abDGCs to alter hippocampal oscillation patterns may be critical for their contribution on behavioral performance (Buzsáki, 2010; Rangel et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buzsáki, 2010, Rangel et al., 2013, and Rangel et al., 2014.

claim: The ability for abDGCs to alter hippocampal oscillation patterns may be critical for their contribution on behavioral performance.
source: As oscillations represent coordinated interactions of excitation and inhibition in a circuit that may create optimal windows for communication, the ability for abDGCs to alter hippocampal oscillation patterns may be critical for their contribution on behavioral performance (Buzsáki, 2010; Rangel et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the relationship between oscillations and behavior, supported by citations.

claim: abDGCs biophysical and synaptic properties relate to their neural network contributions and subsequent behavioral influence.
source: We observed that abDGCs can engage contralateral hippocampal neural network and influence spatial discrimination at a time that largely parallels the transient developmental period of elevated membrane excitability and enhanced synaptic plasticity characterized by in vitro studies (Ge et al., 2007; Gu et al., 2012; Dieni et al., 2013). However, it is unclear how abDGCs biophysical and synaptic properties relate to their neural network contributions and subsequent behavioral influence.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the temporal correlation between biophysical properties and behavioral effects.

claim: Young abDGCs may affect overall DG neuronal excitability non-selectively through gross recruitment of hilar inhibitory neural networks.
source: Intriguing hypotheses have suggested that young abDGCs may affect overall DG neuronal excitability non-selectively through gross recruitment of hilar inhibitory neural networks as described earlier (Jung and McNaughton, 1993; Ikrar et al., 2013; Piatti et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jung and McNaughton, 1993, Ikrar et al., 2013, and Piatti et al., 2013.

claim: Young abDGCs may themselves selectively encode information important for behavioral performance through experience dependent tuning of integration into relevant neural networks.
source: Intriguing hypotheses have suggested that young abDGCs may affect overall DG neuronal excitability non-selectively through gross recruitment of hilar inhibitory neural networks as described earlier (Jung and McNaughton, 1993; Ikrar et al., 2013; Piatti et al., 2013), or that young abDGCs may themselves selectively encode information important for behavioral performance through experience dependent tuning of integration into relevant neural networks (Aimone et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Aimone et al., 2009.

claim: Optogenetic silencing of naive young abDGCs at 5–10 weeks of maturation failed to impair behavioral performance measured either by trial to criteria to complete the illumination block or by success rates for individual laser illumination trials.
source: We first completely trained a cohort of mice to perform the location discrimination task, and then injected retrovirus MSCV-ArchT-GFP or control MSCV-GFP to label abDGCs that were naïve to the task. Optogenetic silencing of naive young abDGCs at 5–10 weeks of maturation failed to impair behavioral performance measured either by trial to criteria to complete the illumination block [repeated measures two-way ANOVA, no significant illumination effect: F1,9 = 2.547, p=0.15; group effect F1,9 = 1.02, p=0.34; mice group × illumination interaction: F1,9 = 0.18, p=0.68], or by success rates for individual laser illumination trials [repeated measures two-way ANOVA, no significant illumination effect: F1,9 = 0.30, p=0.60; group effect F1,9 = 0.12, p=0.74; mice group × illumination interaction: F1,9 = 0.82, p=0.39] (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Retrovirus labeled an identical number of abDGCs in the naïve group compared to the longitudinal group.
source: Compared to that in the longitudinal group, retrovirus labeled an identical number of abDGCs in the naïve group, confirming that the lack of a behavioral deficit in the naïve group cannot be explained by the number of labeled abDGCs (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1.

claim: Although naïve young abDGCs are capable of altering neural networks detectable by fMRI and electrophysiological measurements, their impact on behavioral performance is highly preferential to the networks they are recruited into during the learning experience.
source: Together, these results suggest that although naïve young abDGCs are capable of altering neural networks detectable by fMRI and electrophysiological measurements (Figures 4, 5, and 6), their impact on behavioral performance is highly preferential to the networks they are recruited into during the learning experience (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing network effects without behavioral effects in naive cells.

claim: Although abDGCs may play important roles in non-selectively modulating DG neural network excitability, they preferentially influence certain behavioral aspects, likely through experience-dependent shaping during their neural integration.
source: These findings demonstrate that although abDGCs may play important roles in non-selectively modulating DG neural network excitability, they preferentially influence certain behavioral aspects, likely through experience-dependent shaping during their neural integration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing learning-dependent behavioral effects.

claim: abDGCs during an early development period (5–10 weeks after birth) are highly effective in influencing spatial discrimination and recruiting large scale neural networks involving the bilateral hippocampus.
source: Here we demonstrate that abDGCs, during an early development period, are highly effective in influencing spatial discrimination and recruiting large scale neural networks involving the bilateral hippocampus. The developmental period identified here, 5–10 weeks after birth, largely parallels the time course when abDGCs exhibit heightened membrane excitability and elevated synaptic plasticity as characterized in vitro (Ge et al., 2007; Marín-Burgin et al., 2012; Dieni et al., 2013; Kropff et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Ge et al., 2007, Marín-Burgin et al., 2012, Dieni et al., 2013, and Kropff et al., 2015.

claim: abDGCs have a specialized role for contributing to dentate function, and in particular, young abDGCs, in enhancing DG's pattern separation ability.
source: Our data also parallel other studies in that we find a specialized role for abDGCs in contributing to dentate function, and in particular, young abDGCs, in enhancing DG's pattern separation ability (Ge et al., 2007; Clelland et al., 2009; Sahay et al., 2011a, 2011b; Kesner et al., 2014; Rangel et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Ge et al., 2007, Clelland et al., 2009, Sahay et al., 2011a, 2011b, Kesner et al., 2014, and Rangel et al., 2014.

claim: Task acquisition coincident with development and maturation is an important contributor in determining if abDGCs will influence spatial location performance.
source: Although previous behavioral studies have reported age-dependent influences of abDGCs (Gu et al., 2012; Nakashiba et al., 2012; Swan et al., 2014), our findings add to this discussion by demonstrating that task acquisition coincident with development and maturation is an important contributor in determining if abDGCs will influence spatial location performance.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Gu et al., 2012, Nakashiba et al., 2012, and Swan et al., 2014.

claim: Experience shapes survival, maturation and synapse formation during abDGCs development.
source: It has been well demonstrated that experience shapes survival, maturation and synapse formation during abDGCs development (Tashiro et al., 2007; Rangel et al., 2014; Bergami et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tashiro et al., 2007, Rangel et al., 2014, and Bergami et al., 2015.

claim: The learning dependent behavioral impact supports the rational that abDGCs have dynamical connectivity and their integration within hippocampal networks is highly plastic, and subject to modulation through interactions with the environment.
source: Our study suggests that these considerations also can be applied to neurons recruited into task-relevant networks. The learning dependent behavioral impact further supports the rational that abDGCs have dynamical connectivity and their integration within hippocampal networks is highly plastic, and subject to modulation through interactions with the environment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing learning-dependent effects.

claim: Within the observed developmental window, abDGCs biophysical properties ultimately determine their neural network impact through strategic and learning dependent placement of synaptic connections, beyond nonspecific modulation of local networks.
source: It is reasonable to conclude that within the observed developmental window, abDGCs biophysical properties ultimately determine their neural network impact through strategic and learning dependent placement of synaptic connections, beyond nonspecific modulation of local networks (e.g., through regulating overall levels of feedback inhibition [Amaral et al., 2007; Myers and Scharfman, 2009]).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citations to Amaral et al., 2007 and Myers and Scharfman, 2009.

claim: Enrichment or behavioral training can influence abDGC survival rate, as well as tune their activity patterns to be more selective and dedicated to familiar experiences.
source: Other studies have indicated that enrichment or behavioral training can influence abDGC survival rate, as well as tune their activity patterns to be more selective and dedicated to familiar experiences.
evidence: The claim is based on other studies mentioned in the discussion.

claim: abDGCs could facilitate pattern separation via experience and learning dependent integration into specific task relevant neural networks.
source: Based on these findings, it is plausible that abDGCs could facilitate pattern separation via experience and learning dependent integration into specific task relevant neural networks (Tashiro et al., 2007; Aimone et al., 2009; Rangel et al., 2014; Bergami et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tashiro et al., 2007, Aimone et al., 2009, Rangel et al., 2014, and Bergami et al., 2015.

claim: Only when silencing young abDGCs during the 6–8 week window, but not later on, did significant changes occur in the contralateral hippocampal regions.
source: Toward this endeavor, we employed fMRI and electrophysiology techniques to measure network influences across the maturation windows explored in our behavioral studies. It was only when we silenced young abDGCs during the 6–8 week window, but not later on, did we see significant changes in the contralateral hippocampal regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI and electrophysiology data.

claim: Electrophysiological analysis of the contralateral hippocampus revealed broad changes in the power across a number of frequency bands during optogenetic silencing of young abDGCs.
source: Electrophysiological analysis of the contralateral hippocampus also revealed broad changes in the power across a number of frequency bands during optogenetic silencing of young abDGCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: The LFP effects reached significance in CA1, presumably because of the expansive level of divergence from CA3 to CA1.
source: Although we saw a general rise in power in CA3, the LFP effects reached significance in CA1, presumably because of the expansive level of divergence from CA3 to CA1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the electrophysiology data and anatomical knowledge.

claim: CA3 pyramidal cells make 13 k–28 k synaptic connections with CA1 pyramidal cells, and each CA3 cell contacts between 4–8% of all CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: CA3 pyramidal cells make 13 k–28 k synaptic connections with CA1 pyramidal cells, and each CA3 cell contacts between 4–8% of all CA1 pyramidal cells (Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bezaire and Soltesz, 2013.

claim: The increase in dominant 30–200 Hz rhythms in CA1 fields occurred without CA3 synchrony at those same frequencies.
source: The increase in dominant 30–200 Hz rhythms in CA1 fields also occurred without CA3 synchrony at those same frequencies (Middleton and McHugh, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Middleton and McHugh, 2016.

claim: Only the young population had the ability to regulate the hippocampus bilaterally based on electrophysiology and fMRI experiments.
source: It is intriguing that only the young population had the ability to regulate the hippocampus bilaterally based on our electrophysiology and fMRI experiments.
evidence: The claim is supported by fMRI and electrophysiology data.

claim: Young abDGCs are easier to stimulate in slice electrophysiology studies.
source: For example, young abDGCs are easier to stimulate in slice electrophysiology studies (Ge et al., 2007; Dieni et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ge et al., 2007 and Dieni et al., 2013.

claim: Young abDGCs are believed to exhibit higher firing rates.
source: For example, young abDGCs are easier to stimulate in slice electrophysiology studies (Ge et al., 2007; Dieni et al., 2013) and are believed to exhibit higher firing rates (McHugh et al., 2007; Deng et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McHugh et al., 2007 and Deng et al., 2010.

claim: The majority of the DG granule cells, the developmentally-born ones, exhibit low baseline firing rates of under 0.5 Hz.
source: whereas the majority of the DG granule cells, the developmentally-born ones, exhibit low baseline firing rates of under 0.5 Hz (Jung and McNaughton, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Jung and McNaughton, 1993.

claim: Silencing the highly active young abDGCs could produce a significant downstream network effect that is not present when silencing low firing older granule cells.
source: Therefore, silencing the highly active young abDGCs could produce a significant downstream network effect that is not present when silencing low firing older granule cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differences in firing rates between young and old cells.

claim: Young abDGCs may exhibit unique connectivity patterns, such as preferential connections to interneuron populations.
source: Another possibility is that young abDGCs may exhibit unique connectivity patterns, such as preferential connections to interneuron populations.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on anatomical considerations.

claim: Dentate GCs send the largest number of their inputs to hilar inhibitory neurons.
source: Dentate GCs send the largest number of their inputs to hilar inhibitory neurons (Acsády et al., 1998)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Acsády et al., 1998.

claim: Silencing young active cells could lead to widespread disinhibition of the hippocampus.
source: therefore it is plausible that silencing young active cells could lead to widespread disinhibition of the hippocampus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the connectivity patterns and experimental results.

claim: Enhancing neurogenesis lead to an increase in synaptic connections of newborn neurons specifically onto hilar interneurons.
source: This interpretation is supported by a follow up study where Ikrar et al. (2013) found that enhancing neurogenesis lead to an increase in synaptic connections of newborn neurons specifically onto hilar interneurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ikrar et al., 2013.

claim: Ablation of adult neurogenesis leads to enhanced feedforward excitation to CA3 from existing mature GCs.
source: Interestingly, ablation of adult neurogenesis also leads to enhanced feedforward excitation to CA3 from existing mature GCs.
evidence: The claim is based on findings from other studies mentioned in the discussion.

claim: The increases in hippocampal network activity following x-ray irradiation is not likely due to plasticity changes associated with the loss of these neurons.
source: Our findings add insight into these competing hypotheses in that the increases in hippocampal network activity following x-ray irradiation is not likely due to plasticity changes associated with the loss of these neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the immediate effects observed during optogenetic silencing.

claim: Optogenetic silencing produced changes in the LFP power that ramped as silencing persisted with the end of the silencing window showing enhanced excitability when compared to the early window.
source: We found that optogenetic silencing produced changes in the LFP power that ramped as silencing persisted with the end of the silencing window showing enhanced excitability when compared to the early window.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: Ablation of neurogenesis leads to a reduction in inhibitory input into existing granule cells of the DG.
source: In support of this argument, Singer et al. (2011) described that ablation of neurogenesis also leads to a reduction in inhibitory input into existing granule cells of the DG.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Singer et al., 2011.

claim: Young cells, due to their highly active state, normally contribute to a strong inhibitory tone through hilar neuron connectivity, which is lost during transient optogenetic silencing.
source: Our data combined with other lines of evidence noted above supports a model where young cells, due to their highly active state, normally contribute to a strong inhibitory tone through hilar neuron connectivity, which is lost during transient optogenetic silencing.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and other cited evidence.

claim: The released inhibition leads to a state where unregulated perforant path input promotes an increase in excitability that is conveyed throughout the hippocampal network.
source: The released inhibition leads to a state where unregulated perforant path input promotes an increase in excitability that is conveyed throughout the hippocampal network.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and proposed mechanism.

claim: Recruitment of abDGCs would lead to a sparse firing condition within the DG, in which only the most highly trained inputs overcome inhibition prioritizing input specificity in the face of similar competing inputs.
source: Importantly, this result also adds insight into the role that young cells play in inhibiting the hippocampus during periods of pattern separation. During such performance, recruitment of abDGCs would lead to a sparse firing condition within the DG, in which only the most highly trained inputs overcome inhibition prioritizing input specificity in the face of similar competing inputs. (Jung and McNaughton, 1993; Alme et al., 2010; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2012; Ikrar et al., 2013; Piatti et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citations to Jung and McNaughton, 1993, Alme et al., 2010, Neunuebel and Knierim, 2012, Ikrar et al., 2013, and Piatti et al., 2013.

claim: Pattern separation, in part, is thought to involve the ability to discriminate highly similar inputs into separate and non-overlapping representations.
source: As pattern separation, in part, is thought to involve the ability to discriminate highly similar inputs into separate and non-overlapping representations (Kheirbek et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kheirbek et al., 2012.

claim: The loss of global inhibition associated with reduced activity of young GCs could contribute to a decline in input specificity necessary for pattern separation.
source: the loss of global inhibition associated with reduced activity of young GCs could contribute to a decline in input specificity necessary for pattern separation (Sahay et al., 2011a).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citation to Sahay et al., 2011a.

claim: abDGC influence cells with direct connectivity to CA3 pyramidal cells.
source: It is possible that abDGC influence cells with direct connectivity to CA3 pyramidal cells which has recently been proposed (Temprana et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Temprana et al., 2015.

claim: Silencing young abDGCs may lead to large network changes in the CA3 network that further recruit the contralateral hippocampus through the hippocampal commissure.
source: Under this scenario, silencing young abDGCs may lead to large network changes in the CA3 network that further recruit the contralateral hippocampus through the hippocampal commissure.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on anatomical considerations.

claim: Adult born DGCs may show enhanced connectivity to the contralaterally projecting hilar mossy cell that engage the contralateral CA1.
source: Adult born DGCs may also show enhanced connectivity to the contralaterally projecting hilar mossy cell that engage the contralateral CA1 (Christian et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Christian et al., 2014.

claim: Young adult-born dentate granule cells have a remarkable and previously undefined role in influencing spatial pattern discrimination networks.
source: Taken together, our findings highlight a remarkable and previously undefined role for young adult-born dentate granule cells in influencing spatial pattern discrimination networks.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Young adult-born neurons are recruited into task-relevant networks in an experience-dependent manner.
source: We found that these neurons are recruited into task-relevant networks in an experience-dependent manner, which highlights a role for the importance of ongoing neurogenesis in adulthood.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Young adult-born neurons specifically had the ability to recruit and influence large neural networks including the bilateral hippocampus.
source: We also found that this cell population specifically, had the ability to recruit and influence large neural networks including the bilateral hippocampus.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: The influence of young abDGCs is well suited for mediating cognitive flexibility in the DG circuits.
source: This provides in part, a mechanistic explanation for how such a small number of cells can so broadly impact behavior performance and offers insight into how the influence of young abDGCs is well suited for mediating cognitive flexibility in the DG circuits (Burghardt et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citation to Burghardt et al., 2012.

claim: A reduction in neurogenesis associated with aging or neurological disease can be related to discontinuities in hippocampal networks more broadly.
source: These findings may lead to novel perspectives on how adult neurogenesis modulates hippocampal functions and how a reduction in neurogenesis associated with aging or neurological disease can be related to discontinuities in hippocampal networks more broadly.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on the experimental findings.

claim: Adult-born neurons promote location discrimination during early stages of development but only if they undergo maturation during task acquisition.
source: We discovered that adult-born neurons promote location discrimination during early stages of development but only if they undergo maturation during task acquisition.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Silencing of young adult-born neurons produced changes extending to the contralateral hippocampus, detectable by both electrophysiology and fMRI measurements.
source: Silencing of young adult-born neurons also produced changes extending to the contralateral hippocampus, detectable by both electrophysiology and fMRI measurements
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Young neurons may modulate location discrimination through influences on bilateral hippocampal networks.
source: suggesting young neurons may modulate location discrimination through influences on bilateral hippocampal networks.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental findings.
